item.title: Loneliness Is a Psychiatric Story
item.description:
Loneliness

Loneliness Is a Psychiatric Story

When isolation isn’t just a side effect, it can accelerate mental illness.

Posted August 26, 2026

Key points
  • Loneliness does not merely accompany mental illness—research now suggests it helps cause it.
  • A 2026 review found loneliness significantly predicted the later incidence of psychosis.
  • The effects of prolonged isolation closely mimic the symptoms of mental illness itself.
  • A treatment system that ignores the social dimension of illness leaves the accelerant in place.
Source: Zoshua Colah/Pixabay

In the decade between my first manic break and my arrest on felony charges, I occupied a kind of social quarantine. The details shifted—whether living with a father whose facility to express emotions was gradually erased by Parkinson’s, or living alone with my two dogs and a proliferation of screens and substances—but the underlying absence was constant. I was lonely, profoundly so. Yet no clinician who saw me across countless hospitalizations, a county jail, and a state forensic psychiatric institution ever isolated that solitude as a clinical variable worthy of discussion.

When I shared an apartment with my father, even as I knew we still loved each other, we lacked the capacity to connect. Both of our illnesses—his Parkinson’s and my untreated bipolar disorder—robbed us as much of the ability to transmit warmth as the readiness to receive it. Instead, like far too many today, we retreated into our phones, and the silence between us grew structural. Once he transitioned to assisted living, even that semblance of an emotional architecture collapsed. A Rottweiler and a Beagle became my social world, and I tried to convince myself that their companionship—our long meditative walks around the lakes—was enough. It never was.

It is not surprising that the clinicians who saw me failed to account for the role of loneliness, because our mental health system, by design, focuses on biology: the medication check, the symptom checklist, the diagnostic code. Most experts pay lip service to George Engel’s biopsychosocial model, which insists that the social and psychological dimensions are not an afterthought to mental illness but core components of it. In clinical practice, practitioners especially ignore the social part of that model.

Research, however, has outpaced practice. John Cacioppo showed how sustained loneliness is not simply an emotional state but a physiological one. It raises cortisol, disrupts sleep architecture, diminishes immune function, and—critically—distorts the very social cognition a person needs to reverse the damage. Loneliness engenders more loneliness. For older people navigating serious illness, like my late father, chronic loneliness raises the odds of death in any given year by 26 percent.

The World Health Organization’s 2025 report on social connection unpacks the public health stakes: persistent loneliness not only increases vulnerability to depression and anxiety, but it also erodes the self-concept required to recover from any severe illness.

The implications for psychiatry are as disturbing as they are clear. The effects of pervasive isolation—contortion of self-concept, emotional dysregulation, susceptibility to rumination, paranoia, and even psychosis—closely resemble the symptoms of serious mental illness. This is not a fluke; it is a causal loop. Loneliness disrupts the nervous system; the disruption intensifies psychiatric symptoms; the symptoms, in turn, increase isolation; and the isolation exacerbates the illness. The anthropologist Tanya Luhrmann insists that we frame serious psychiatric disorders as embedded within social relations; mental illness is the product not simply of brain chemistry but of the social world in which that chemistry unfolds. And when we remove the relational world, the illness does not remain inert. It accelerates.

A 2026 systematic review further underscored this causal relationship. In six longitudinal studies, researchers identified a significant association between loneliness and a subsequent incidence of psychosis—not merely correlation but something more like bidirectional causation. The psychiatric genetics researcher Jehannine Austin has poetically described the implication of this evidence: “What separates those of us who do suffer from those of us that don’t is what happens to us during our lives.” Loneliness, ignored to the point that it becomes pervasive, is something that happens to you.

To be clear, my bipolar disorder was not the result of loneliness. But a profound sense of isolation shaped the course of my illness in ways the mental health system routinely ignored. When my correct diagnosis finally arrived in 2020, four years after my first manic episode, my family was not integrated into my discharge plan. I left with the anosognosia still fully intact. I flushed the pills down the toilet and languished for another five years before receiving proper treatment. During that decade, never once did anyone assess whether my social world was meaningfully supportive, whether I had people still in reach, or if the silence I inhabited was deteriorating my condition.

Source: Artem Podrez/Pexels

The problem of loneliness functions on three levels simultaneously. Clinically, mental health care focuses on the palliative reduction of symptoms rather than the slower reconstitution of friendships and families. Patients are seen as atomistic individuals, and the illness is addressed without considering the ecology that surrounds it. Culturally, we have built a world of smartphone stimulation over the complexity of presence. The screen provides a seemingly frictionless substitute for the friction that genuine intimacy requires. For anyone whose nervous system is already disturbed, the addictive warmth of a smartphone is not a neutral haven; it deepens the wound. Globally, loneliness is not recognized as a public health crisis, though the evidence is not contested. But, with rare exceptions like social prescribing in the United Kingdom, we lack a medical system that acts on it.

As I suggested in a recent essay, the most insidious obstacle may be what the research has yet to name: The problem of being present with a mind you do not trust. Luhrmann called this awkward intimacy—the capacity to sit next to someone whose actions have scared you, whose sickness has made them impenetrable or cruel. That unease is real, and it sheds light on why psychiatrists reach for the prescription pad over the therapeutic relationship. Medication is quantifiable and clean. It doesn't ask you to stay in the room and look a person in the eyes whose mind you do not understand.

But the uncomfortable, awkward encounter in a room is where healing takes place. A mental health system that asks whether a patient is dangerous to herself or others but not whether she is loved—whether anyone who knew her before the illness is still present in her life—is a system that has left the accelerant in place while only treating the fire.

item.title: How Music Helps Regulate Our Emotions
item.description:
Emotions

How Music Helps Regulate Our Emotions

The power of your playlists to heal, calm, and energize.

Posted August 26, 2026

Key points
  • Emotion regulation is the ability to effectively manage and respond to an emotional experience.
  • Our ability to manage the flow of thoughts contribute to happiness.
  • Music is a highly valuable tool for emotion regulation.

A prominent view in psychology is that our emotional lives are shaped by our values and judgments. It’s the basic premise of modern cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT). This is also one of the basic psychological principles of Stoicism. Much, if not all, of our thinking is up to us. We can liberate ourselves from destructive emotions such as anger and hatred by developing a capacity to choose how to interpret the situation.

Stimuli (events) > Appraisal (thoughts) > Feelings > Action (tendency)

Source: Image by Pexels from Pixabay

The appraisal aspect of emotion suggests that our emotions are not entirely beyond our control. They do not just happen to us, but we are responsible for them. We interpret everything we see or hear in terms of our habitual thinking or prior experience. Thus, an emotion is a special kind of thinking about what we make of an event. This theory also shapes how we practice emotion regulation. Emotion regulation refers to attempts to influence which emotions one has, when one has them, or how these emotions are experienced or expressed.

Music offers a resource for emotion regulation (Koelsch, 2025). Music is a universal source of enjoyment for humans, and hearing a favorite tune can instantly lift one’s mood. Music can be used to down-regulate negative emotions. Simply immersing ourselves in positive-sounding tunes can break the toxic cycles of negative emotions, filling us with fresh, uplifting thoughts and elevating our mood.

People use music to achieve various goals, such as to energize, maintain focus on tasks, and reduce boredom. For instance, sad music enables the listener to disengage from distressing situations (breakups, death, etc.) and focus instead on the beauty of the music. Further, lyrics that resonate with the listener’s personal experience can give voice to feelings or experiences that one might not be able to express oneself.

Music often creates strong action tendencies to move in coordination with the music (e.g., dancing, foot-tapping). Our internal rhythms (e.g., heart rate) speed up or slow down to become one with the music. We float and move with the music. Dance is a powerful way to express joy and connect with others. In younger individuals suffering from depression, dancing effectively alleviates symptoms of depression and anxiety (Prudente, 2024).

According to the Broaden-and-Build Theory (Fredrickson, 2009), positive emotions result in a broadening of the scope of attention, an increased openness to new experiences, and a readiness to engage in holistic processing. The ability of music to increase positive emotions broadens the listener’s behavioral and cognitive repertoire. Upbeat music can make us perceive the world in a brighter light. Listening to happy music can influence the way one perceives the world in a stressful situation. For example, upbeat tunes can give you an optimistic outlook and make you feel better. Music distracts attention, making it easier to focus on positive thoughts, thus alleviating worries.

Music evokes emotional memories if we have stored it alongside an emotionally significant autobiographical event. Later, listening to this music can trigger the memory and its associated emotion. For example, Christmas songs are associated with childhood memories of the festive spirit and thus inspire feelings of Christmas cheer. One might exploit this phenomenon by organizing a playlist that evokes positive autobiographical memories, thereby activating corresponding uplifting moods.

In sum, music is a highly valuable tool for emotion regulation. Active engagement with preferred music brings on a pleasant state and helps to regulate moods and emotions. Actively interacting with music is essential. By fully focusing on the sound and physically responding through singing, dancing or tapping, you occupy your working memory. Doing so effectively blocks out negative thoughts.

However, music is not a magic pill that can immediately resolve a negative mood. For instance, depressive mood is often closely related to thought patterns. The benefits of listening to distracting music can be temporary. However, listening to music that alters mood via shifting thought patterns may have a long-lasting effect. Also, the effect of music is personal. The same music that stimulates some people to dance may move others to tears. This exclusively depends on the thoughts that are aroused in our memories.

item.title: Break the Stress-Drinking Loop: Upgrade Your Stress Mindset
item.description:
Alcoholism

Break the Stress-Drinking Loop: Upgrade Your Stress Mindset

How negative stress mindsets can fuel an unwanted stress-drinking cycle

Posted August 26, 2026

Key points
  • Limiting beliefs about stress or alcohol can trap people in unwanted drinking loops.
  • Avoiding stress altogether isn’t practical because it’s part of being human.
  • Adopting a positive stress mindset can reduce its negative effects and help break the stress-drinking loop.

For years, I told my clients that it’s important to reduce the amount of stress in recovery. It was the same piece of advice that I was told in my own journey, and it made sense. After all, studies show clear links between stress and an increased risk of relapse. It makes sense that to prevent falling back into an unwanted stress-drinking cycle, one should do their best to reduce stress.

But somehow I always felt uneasy about the advice. Because, deep down, I knew that, as much as the advice sounded good in theory, it wasn’t always practical in practice.

Stress is part of being human

The truth is that stress is part of life. Most of the stress that we face in life is not an extracurricular activity that we take on by choice. Typical stressors are often things not within a person’s control, such as health problems, a sudden loss, or unexpected unemployment. Nor are they things a person can simply opt out of, like a stressful job, pressure at school, or the responsibility of being a parent.

So in a way, I’ve felt like I was giving people advice that wasn’t really rooted in the reality of being human. And on some level, I knew there had to be another way to truly outgrow an unwanted stress-drinking cycle that doesn’t ask a person to create a stress-free environment.

A study that changed my understanding of stress

Finally, the answer came to me through a surprising study that transformed my understanding of stress. For years, I was told that stress not only can increase the risk of relapse, but also can be very harmful to our health.

To better understand the impact stress can have on people’s health, in 1998, a group of researchers asked nearly 30,000 Americans how much stress they had experienced over the past year. Eight years later, they followed up to see whether there was any correlation between the amount of stress a person experienced and their mortality rate. The numbers were alarming: people who reported a high level of stress had a 43 percent higher risk of premature death.

It would be tempting to conclude from this that high levels of stress can literally kill us. Except there was one group that, despite reporting high levels of stress, had a lower mortality rate than even the people who reported very little stress. What made this group seemingly immune to the harmful effects of stress? Everyone couldn’t help but wonder.

The secret lay in the second question that the researchers asked: Did the participants believe that stress was harmful to their health? Some people said yes, while others said no. Eight years later, it turned out that only the people who believed that stress was harmful suffered a higher risk of death. In other words, what makes stress so harmful may not be the stress itself but a person’s mindset toward it.

It got me thinking: What if the thing that pulls a person back into the stress-drinking loop is not stress itself, but one’s mindset around stress?

How limiting mindsets keep us stuck in an unwanted drinking cycle

Mindset intervention has always been a core part of my work in helping a person outgrow an old drinking pattern. Through my years of personal journey and professional work, I’ve come to see the important role that a mindset can play in either reinforcing or interrupting an unwanted drinking pattern.

A mindset is an invisible filter that we see everything through. It shapes how we think, feel, and act. It determines how we interpret experiences and influences the decisions that we make. A limiting mindset about one’s ability to grow beyond their struggle with alcohol often hinders progress and keeps a person stuck in an old drinking pattern, whereas a supportive mindset tends to allow a person to remain resilient and resourceful when facing challenges.

Invisible Drinking Loop
Source: Jeanette Hu | Sober Curiosity

In my work, limiting mindsets are seen as one of the four core invisible forces that keep a person stuck in what I call an “invisible drinking loop.” For example, a limiting mindset that says, “If I slip, I have failed,” makes a person more likely to feel discouraged and give up after a setback, and the belief, “I have a diseased brain,” makes a person more likely to interpret the inevitable challenges of breaking an old drinking pattern as proof of their inability to change and grow. Unfortunately, the mainstream narratives about addiction and recovery often unintentionally feed these unhelpful mindsets.

First step to break a stress-drinking loop: Upgrade your stress mindset

The stress study made me realize that the limiting mindsets that can fuel an unwanted drinking pattern aren’t restricted to one’s mindset around sobriety and recovery.

When it comes to our stress mindset, a mainstream culture that overemphasizes the harmful effects of stress often creates fear around stress and motivates avoidance. However, because many everyday stressors cannot be easily removed from our lives, we become compelled to find ways to remove them from our minds, including turning to alcohol to forget our troubles. This need to seek quick relief from stress becomes the fuel for the stress-drinking loop, an unwanted drinking cycle where drinking starts as an attempt to seek relief from stress, then gradually becomes the default response to stressful situations.

Therefore, to truly put an end to the stress-drinking loop, the key may not lie in trying to create a stress-free life but in developing a more positive mindset toward stress. This begins with learning new ways to respond to stress. To explore this further, you can start with these three simple strategies to lean into your stress response.
